extracted.intended_audience: researchers, program officers, and academics interested in grant peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, norms, and evaluative criteria governing academic grant peer-review panels, including interactional norms, methodological standards, and procedural influences on funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting other panelists' opinions / collegiality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Respecting other panelists’ opinions is an essential quality of a good panelist. Being respectful upholds the customary rule of collegiality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upholding collegiality prevents personal offense and preserves the panel’s ability to deliberate. Breaches (direct, 'in your face' responses) create discomfort and can produce open conflict, exclusion, or prolonged upset (examples: a panelist eating alone after a dispute). Chairs and program officers should manage breaches to maintain collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion work / saving face and reintegration
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers, panel chairs, and some panelists engage in “emotion work,” helping colleagues save face even after defeat and reintegrating them into the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active management of interpersonal damage (reassurances, face-saving moves, moderated critiques) is a deliberate task to sustain productive deliberation across the two-day panel; failure to perform emotion work risks derailing further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding non-articulated or performative objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Mut ed expressions of enthusiasm (frowning, rolling eyes, sighing, talking through clenched teeth) and allusive objections dampen debate because they are not amenable to contestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms should be explicit and contestable; reliance on gestures or innuendo undermines fair deliberation. Chairs should discourage passive-aggressive behavior and encourage clearly stated objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent criteria across proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Maintaining consistent criteria for judging qualitative and quantitative proposals is crucial to panel legitimacy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists should ask consistent kinds of questions across proposals (e.g., clarity of research design, mapping of relationships, consideration of alternative explanations). Be aware that standards can drift as panels compare different batches; explicit cross-checking (revisiting best/worst items) helps preserve consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect cognitive contextualization / disciplinary sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: To respect 'cognitive contextualization' means to adopt different criteria of evaluation for different proposals—applying the most appropriate disciplinary criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists should apply disciplinary-appropriate standards (e.g., what counts as ethnography varies by discipline). This requires flexibility but must be balanced against the demand for consistency; chairs should clarify when disciplinary-specific criteria are being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let topic appeal override methodological standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels may be tempted to overlook standard rules because a topic is enticing; conflicts arise when enthusiasm for a topic leads members to excuse methodological flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criteria (e.g., feasibility, clarity of methods, testing strategy) should not be waived solely for an attractive topic. Deliberations should explicitly address whether to prioritize novelty/ambition over methodological rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base decisions on dossier materials; avoid gossip and reputational innuendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists should be urged 'to make their decision on the basis of the materials before them as opposed to going beyond that.' Gossip and innuendo about applicants (e.g., reputation, advances from publishers) should not substitute for dossier evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage appeals to applicant reputation or off-record information. If reputation-based claims arise, require that they be supported by dossier evidence before influencing funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket self-interest / avoid strategic self-serving behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Following customary rules includes bracketing self-interest; breaches (e.g., overt clientelism or horse-trading) offend panelists’ sense of appropriateness and can undermine legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists should disclose potential conflicts and avoid advocating solely to benefit their own projects or constituents. Chairs should monitor and discourage overt strategic trading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage uneven personal influence and pecking order effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A pecking order emerges: some members are listened to more and sway outcomes; dominance, tone, and perceived authority (institutional affiliation, personality) shape deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all have a chance to speak; watch for domination by charismatic or high-status members. Chairs should enable quieter or lower-status panelists to contribute and should question assertions presented as definitive because of who made them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of institutional prestige and similarity-based influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional affiliation (e.g., Ivy League) and intellectual similarity can grant disproportionate weight to panelists’ opinions; shared theoretical frameworks may legitimize mutual influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when judgments are influenced by prestige or intellectual affinity; treat similarity as a legitimate heuristic only when substantiated by argument, and avoid allowing affiliation to substitute for evidence-based critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and mitigate gender, race, and seniority biases in influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Gendered and racialized expectations affect how much influence panelists exercise; women and minorities may face low expectations or different performance pressures (e.g., advice to adopt a more bombastic style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should be conscious of differential expectations and interactional disadvantages; chairs should actively solicit input from those who defer and guard against dismissing contributions based on gender or race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for preexisting networks and reputational information
rubrics_metrics.description: Preexisting personal ties, reputations, or indirect connections among panelists can influence deliberation dynamics and the weight given to opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, disclose prior relationships; be cautious about letting informal networks determine whose views are trusted. Recognize that panels often lack full information about colleagues, which can accentuate disciplinary stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge chance, timing, and sequence effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomness and order effects matter: who is on the panel, the order proposals are discussed (alphabetical or by batch), and when during the meeting a proposal is heard can change outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedures to mitigate order effects (e.g., randomize order, revisit early/late decisions); be cautious about decisions made late in the day when fatigue and pressure to finish may bias outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rushed decisions due to time pressure and intellectual exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists experience intellectual exhaustion after two days; near the end they may negotiate quickly, make less rigorous judgments, or make awards without apparent merit-based displacement effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sufficient time allocation, consider mechanisms for reconsideration, and resist finishing under time pressure. Chairs should monitor energy levels and guard against joke-making or trivialization when fatigue sets in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clear research design and explicit consideration of alternative explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging proposals, look for a research design that is fairly explicit about the claims being made: the exact relationships to be mapped and which alternative explanations are being considered or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposals on clarity of design, specification of relationships, operationalization, and explicit handling of alternatives; request clarifications where designs are vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept inevitability of idiosyncratic evaluations but make them contestable
rubrics_metrics.description: Idiosyncratic evaluations are almost unavoidable, yet are often presented as universalistic and woven into formal criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge subjectivity and require that idiosyncratic judgments be justified with reasons that others can contest or evaluate, rather than asserted as universal truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect customary deliberative rules to accumulate credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Respecting the customary rules of deliberations is crucial for accumulating credibility with co-panelists (a necessary condition for making one’s label 'stick' to a proposal) and for facilitating deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to norms (bracketing self-interest, collegiality, explicitness of critique) because following them influences how arguments are heard and the panel’s overall legitimacy; breaches weaken the panel’s effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand evaluation as interactional and emotional, not purely cognitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of evaluating is an eminently interactional and emotional undertaking, rather than a cognitive process corrupted by extra-cognitive factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for emotional and interactional dynamics in panel design and chairing practices (e.g., provide structures to manage emotion, reduce personal antagonism, and facilitate reasoned exchange).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design deliberation procedures to expose and correct inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards saliency varies across proposals and batches; panelists’ standards 'evolve' as they work through a batch, sometimes creating inconsistent application of criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement procedures (periodic recalibration, revisiting earlier ratings, explicit criteria lists) to expose drift and keep standards aligned across the whole set of applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about and minimize effects of randomness on innovative proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovative, quirky, or daring proposals (the 'alternates') are especially vulnerable to random and process-driven variables (committee interactions, alphabetical order, timing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give extra attention to potentially high-risk/high-reward proposals (e.g., extended discussion, separate scoring rubric for innovation) and consider safeguards to protect promising unconventional work from being lost to process noise.
